parole.significato: to get underway and pick up speed (of a boat or aircraft)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan abrivar.
Probably from Old Occitan afanar, with cognates Catalan afanyar, afanar and Spanish afanar. Arabic and Vulgar Latin origins have been suggested, but uncertain.
Borrowed from Old Occitan agradar.

parole.significato: to put at ease, to accommodate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan aizar and/or Old French aisier. By surface analysis, agio + -are.

Borrowed from Old Occitan aize, from Vulgar Latin *adjace(m), from Latin adjacēns, present participle of adjaceō (compare Medieval Latin in aiace). Cognate with Old French aise, eise, French aise and aisance; compare also Catalan eina. Doublet of adiacente.
Borrowed from Old Occitan agulha, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”) (whence Italian ago). Doublet of agucchia, now rare. Compare Sicilian agugghia.
Old Italian, from Old Occitan ambaissada, from Gaulish ambaxtos.
Inherited from Old Italian ambassadore, from Old Occitan ambaisador.

From Old Occitan amistat, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”). Attested since the 1240s, a regular apocope of Old Italian amistade (as a personal name since 12th c.). Eventually replaced by the Latinism amicizia. Compare Sicilian amistà and amistati.
Borrowed from Old Occitan austor, from Vulgar Latin *acceptōrem, modification of Latin accipiter (“hawk”). Unlikely to derive from Latin astŭrem (“type of hawk”), considering its stress position.
From Old Occitan auzel, from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”). Doublet of uccello, the native counterpart. Compare Sicilian auceḍḍu.
From Old Occitan, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bindā (“tie, join, link”). Compare French bande.
Borrowed from Old Occitan batalh, from Vulgar Latin *bat(t)uāculum. Synonym and doublet of batacchio, which was inherited from the same source. Cognate with Sicilian battagghiu.
From Old Occitan beltat, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem, derived from Latin bellus (“beautiful”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan benenanza.
Derived from (or related to) the same stratum of Old Occitan briu (“wild”), from Gaulish *brīgos (“strength”), from Proto-Celtic *brīgos (“importance”). Compare Sicilian sbriguni, Spanish brío.

Borrowed from Old Occitan bauzia, from Old Frankish *bausī (“deceit”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin *bauscia (compare also Friulian bausie, Dalmatian bosca, Old French boisie), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“puffed up, arrogant, bad”). Cognate with Dutch boos, German böse, English boast
Perhaps from Old Occitan bobansa and burban or burbero.
From Old Occitan carpentier, from Late Latin carpentārius (“carpenter”), from Latin carpentārius (“wagon-maker, carriage-maker”).

Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or its variants (compare modern Occitan carrièra, also French carrière), from Late Latin carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet carraia, now archaic.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier (cf. also Old French chevalier), from Late Latin caballārius. See cavallo + -iere. Doublet of cavallaio.

Borrowed from Old Occitan cavilla (compare modern cavilha), from Vulgar Latin *cāvic(u)la, from Classical Latin clāvicula, diminutive of clāvis (“key”). Compare the doublets cavicchia (inherited from Latin), clavicola (borrowed from Latin).
From Old Occitan colobrina, derived from Classical Latin coluber (“snake”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.
Borrowed from Old Occitan dezirar, from Latin dēsīderāre (“to want, desire”). Doublet of desiderare.
Borrowed from Old Occitan dezire.

Borrowed from Old Occitan donçela, donsela, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, from Classical Latin domina (“mistress”), from domus (“house”), from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, from root *dem- (“to build”). Doublet of damigella.
Borrowed from Old Occitan donçel, donzel, donsel, from Vulgar Latin *domnicellus, from Classical Latin dominus.
Borrowed from Old Occitan drut, from Medieval Latin drudus, from Proto-Germanic *drūdaz (“dear, beloved”) (German traut).
Probably from Old Occitan falb, from Old High German falo, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz. Compare French fauve (“tawny”) and English fallow.

parole.significato: a small fortress; a fortalice, fort
parole.testo: From Old Occitan fortaleza.
From Old Occitan frontiera, from front. Compare French frontière.
Borrowed from Old Occitan gent, from Latin [homō] gentis (“[man] of noble family”).
From Old Occitan joglar.
Borrowed from Old Occitan governal, from Latin gubernāculum.

parole.significato: a rotating wire- or fibreglass brush used by jewellery-makers to polish gold or silver
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan grataboyssa.
Borrowed from Old Occitan guaita, from Old High German wahta, from Proto-West Germanic *wahtu, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō (“watch; vigil”), derived from *wakaną (“to wake; to be awake”).

From Old Occitan, from Old French guant, from Frankish *want, from Proto-Germanic *wantuz (“glove, mitten”), from Proto-Indo-European *wondʰnú- (“glove”), from the root *wendʰ- (“to wind, wrap”). Cognates include French gant, Catalan guant, Sicilian nguanta and Spanish guante.
Apheretic of aguglia, borrowed from Old Occitan agulha, from Late Latin acūcula, a diminutive of Latin acus (“needle, pin”).
From Old Occitan guidar, of Germanic origin; e.g. Frankish *witan, Proto-Germanic *witaną, possibly through a Medieval Latin intermediary. Compare French guider, Spanish guiar.
From Old Occitan guidon, related to guidare (“to drive”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan enveja, from Latin invidia. Cognate with Sicilian mmija.
Borrowed from Old Occitan lampan.
Borrowed from Old Occitan or Old French leial, from Latin legālis, whence also the doublet legale.
Borrowed from Old Occitan leujairia, derived from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis (“light (not heavy)”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan lenguatge and adapted to Italian lingua. By surface analysis, lingua + -aggio.
Borrowed from Old Occitan lauzenga, from Frankish *lausungu.
From Old Occitan maestral, from Late Latin magistrālis (ventus) (“master (wind)”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan malha, from Latin macula (“mesh”). Compare Spanish malla, French maille and Portuguese malha.
Borrowed from Old Occitan malvatz, from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”). Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese malvado, and more distantly with French mauvais.
Borrowed from Old Occitan maisnada, from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, derived from Latin mānsiō.

parole.significato: to brand (to mark cattle with as proofof ownership)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan mercar, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *markōną (“to mark; to notice”).

parole.significato: form of address equivalent to signore
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan meser. Cognate to French monsieur.
Borrowed from Old Occitan miralh, ultimately derived from Latin mīrārī (“gaze at”).

parole.significato: to moult (to shed and replace feathers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan mudar, from Latin mūtāre (“to change”). Doublet of mutare.
Borrowed from Old Occitan enemistat, from Vulgar Latin *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus, based on inimīcitia.
Probably from Old Occitan enoja, from enojar, ultimately from Latin inodiō. See more at annoiare. Cognate with French ennui, Spanish enojo, Portuguese nojo and Galician noxo.
Borrowed from Old Occitan enojos.
Borrowed from Old Occitan oltracuidan, Old French outrecuidiant.
Borrowed from Old Occitan auripel, Old French oripel, from Latin aurea pellis (literally “golden skin”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan ploja, from Vulgar Latin *ploia, *plovia, from Classical Latin pluvia (“rain”). Doublet of piova and pioggia.
From Old Occitan preguiera, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem. Cognate with Sicilian prijera.
Borrowed from Old Occitan rai, from Latin radius. Doublet of raggio, razzo, and radio, the first two of which were inherited from Latin, while the last was borrowed from Latin.
From Old Occitan rebeca, from Arabic رَبَاب (rabāb, “rabab”).

parole.significato: to escape, to flee, to take refuge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan repairar, itself from Late Latin repatriāre (“return to one's country”), from Latin patria.
From Old Occitan rossinhol, from Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, derived from Latin luscinia. Same source as usignolo.
From Old Occitan savi, from Vulgar Latin *sapium (“wise”), from Latin sapidus (“delicious, wise”). Doublet of sapido, a borrowing from Latin.

parole.significato: to dismay, dumbfound, make someone's jaw drop
parole.testo: Probably from Old Occitan esbair or Old French esbahir.

Borrowed from Old Occitan esquiera, from Old French eschiere, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarō, whence also Old English sċearu, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to part; split; cut off; sever; divide”). Compare German Schar (“troop”), Danish skare (“host", "crowd”).

Likely from Old Occitan eissalot and its variants (e.g. eyssiroc), from Massalian Ancient Greek *ἐξαλώτης (*exalṓtēs), from ἔξαλος (éxalos, "out of the sea" → "wind from the southeast"). Traditionally thought to be a derivative of Arabic شرق (šarq, “east”). Akin to Italian barocco. Compare Sicilian
Borrowed from Old Occitan esconfire, from Latin *excōnficiō, from ex- + cōnficiō.
Borrowed from Old Occitan escudier, from Late Latin scūtārius, from Latin scūtum. Compare French écuyer.

Borrowed from Old Occitan salvatge, from Vulgar Latin *salvāticus, from Latin silvāticus (“of the woods”). Doublet of the inherited selvatico. Compare Sicilian sarbaggiu, Spanish salvaje, Portuguese selvagem, Catalan salvatge, Piedmontese salvaj.
From earlier semblante, from Old Occitan semblan, semblant, semblanz, present participle of semblar. See also somigliante.
From Old Occitan semblanza, semblança; cf. semblar. Compare also somiglianza.

parole.significato: to seem, to look (like), to appear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan semblar, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). More or less a doublet of somigliare.

parole.significato: to overwhelm, to overpower, to win
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan sobransar, derived from sobrar, from Latin superāre (“to rise over, go over”).

parole.significato: bell (round the neck of cattle etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan sonalh, from Vulgar Latin *sonāculum, from Latin sonāre (“make noise”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).

From Spagna (“Spain”) + -olo (“derivative suffix”), possibly also from Old Occitan espaignol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus, from Latin Hispānus. Compare French espagnol, Portuguese espanhol, Spanish español. Doublet of épagneul.
Borrowed from Old Occitan espelh, from Latin speculum. Doublet of specchio.

parole.significato: a rhythmic instrumental composition that accompanied a poem (in the 13th and 14th centuries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan or Occitan estampida, from estampier, from Gothic *𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌼𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*stampjan), from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, from Proto-Indo-European *stembʰ- (“to trample down”).

parole.significato: a form of eight-line satirical verse
parole.testo: From Old Occitan estrabot, Old French estribot, crossed with strambo.
Probably from Old Occitan esvelhar, from Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre [whence also Old French esveillier], from Latin ēvigilāre.
Borrowed from Old Occitan tensó(n), from Vulgar Latin *tentiōnem, probably from Latin contentiō. Compare Old French tençon (modern French tenson).
Probably from Old Occitan toalha, from Frankish *þwahilu. Cognate with Portuguese toalha (“towel”).

parole.significato: to overflow [with da ‘from’] (of liquid or other material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan trabucar, ultimately from Frankish *būk; with influence from Italian bocca.
From Old Occitan trabuquet. Compare Piedmontese trabucèt, trabücet.
Borrowed from Old Occitan trobar, from Vulgar Latin *tropāre, from Latin tropus.
Derived from Old Occitan trobador, oblique case of trobaire, derived from trobar (“to find”).

Borrowed from Old Occitan urtar, probably a derivation from Frankish *hūrt (“battering ram”), from Proto-Germanic *hrūtaną, *hreutaną (“to fall, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *krew- (“to fall, beat, smash, strike, break”).
From earlier asbergo, from Old Occitan halsberg, from Early Medieval Latin (h)alsbergum, from Frankish *halsaberg (“neck-cover”).

parole.significato: to watch over, to care for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan velhar (cf. Old French veiller), which was inherited from Latin vigilāre. Replaced the original Italian vegghiare, which was inherited from Latin. Also a doublet of vigilare, a learned borrowing from Latin.
Borrowed from Old Occitan vielh. Doublet of vecchio.

Borrowed from Old Occitan viatge and Old French viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum, from the adjective viāticus, from via (“road, path”) + -āticus (“pertaining to”). By surface analysis, via + -aggio. Doublet of viatico and cognate to Catalan viatge, French and English voyage, Spanish viaje, Portugu
Possibly from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), ultimately from Medieval Latin *vitula (“stringed instrument”), which could be related to the goddess Latin vitula.
